etymology: Initialism for just kidding, from 1990s chat rooms and AOL Instant Messenger, where tone was invisible and a sentence could be read as an insult; jk was appended to signal play. The underlying verb, to kid (to tease, to hoax), is nineteenth-century slang from kid (a young goat, then a child): to kid someone was to treat him as a child, to fool him. Texting in the 2000s made jk a reflex, alongside jk jk, jkjk, and the spoken "jay-kay."
biblical_def: JK is the typed wink: a signal that the words before it were not meant seriously. Sometimes it rescues an honest joke from misunderstanding, and that is fine. Often it does something else: it lets a person say what he really thinks and then disown it. "You’re kind of annoying jk." The Christian observation: Scripture has a precise proverb for this exact move. "As a mad man who casteth firebrands, arrows, and death, So is the man that deceiveth his neighbour, and saith, Am not I in sport?" (Pro 26:18-19). The madman is not excused because he says he was playing; the arrow still lands. Jesus said that "every idle word that men shall speak, they shall give account thereof" (Mat 12:36), and James warns that the tongue is "a fire, a world of iniquity" (Jas 3:6). The appended jk does not erase the word; it only refuses responsibility for it. Christian speech aims at the opposite: say what you mean, mean it kindly, and own it. "Speaking the truth in love" (Eph 4:15). Humour is a good gift, and a household can be full of teasing that builds up; the test is whether both people are laughing. A father teaches his children to joke generously, to never use "just kidding" as a shield, and to apologize plainly when a joke wounds instead of retreating behind the initials.
webster_summary: Millennial chat and text initialism (1990s) for just kidding; innocent as a tone marker, sinful as a shield for a real barb, which Proverbs likens to a madman’s firebrand (Pro 26:18-19).
webster_full: JK, interj. (Millennial chat and text slang, 1990s–present; initialism of just kidding) Appended to signal that a preceding remark was a joke. Also jk jk, jkjk, "jay-kay."
Often used to retract a sincere criticism after it has been delivered.
Webster (1828), root kid: KID, noun [Latin hoedus; vulgar.] 1. A young goat. […]
Decode for parents: when "jk" follows a cutting remark, the cut was meant; teach your children to own their words.
scriptures: As a mad man who casteth firebrands, arrows, and death, So is the man that deceiveth his neighbour, and saith, Am not I in sport?
But I say unto you, That every idle word that men shall speak, they shall give account thereof in the day of judgment.
Jas 3:6
And the tongue is a fire, a world of iniquity: so is the tongue among our members, that it defileth the whole body, and setteth on fire the course of nature; and it is set on fire of hell.
Eph 4:15
But speaking the truth in love, may grow up into him in all things, which is the head, even Christ:
Eph 4:29
Let no corrupt communication proceed out of your mouth, but that which is good to the use of edifying, that it may minister grace unto the hearers.
corruption_summary: JK lets a real barb be thrown and disowned in one breath; Scripture calls that the madman’s "Am not I in sport?" and asks for speech owned in truth and love.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is evasion. Online culture made it easy to test an insult and retreat if it landed badly, and jk became the retreat. A child learns that words can be used without being owned, and that the injured party is at fault for "taking it seriously." Proverbs sees through it instantly; the man who deceives his neighbour and calls it sport is as dangerous as one hurling arrows.

The recovery is ownership. "Let no corrupt communication proceed out of your mouth, but that which is good to the use of edifying, that it may minister grace unto the hearers" (Eph 4:29). That leaves plenty of room for laughter, banter, and the teasing of friends who love each other. It leaves no room for the joke that is really an accusation. Teach the young to say plainly what they think, to say it kindly, and when they get it wrong, to say "I was wrong" instead of "jk."
roots_summary: Kid (young goat → child) → 19th-c. to kid (to tease, to fool) → just kidding → 1990s chat initialism jk.
roots_lines: Middle English kide, Old Norse kith — a young goat
19th c. slang: to kid — to treat as a child, to hoax, to tease
1990s: chat and AIM initialism jk; 2000s: texting reflex
Variants: jkjk, jk lol, spoken "jay-kay"
Biblical anchor: Am not I in sport? (Pro 26:19); speaking the truth in love (Eph 4:15)
usage: "Nice haircut jk it’s fine."
The firebrand still burns after the "jk" (Pro 26:18-19).
Say it in love and own it (Eph 4:15).

etymology: Initialism for I don’t know, from 1990s chat and 2000s texting, where it became the all-purpose shrug: ignorance, indecision, indifference, or a refusal to commit ("idk, whatever you want"). Related forms: idek (I don’t even know), idc (I don’t care), idrk (I don’t really know), and the typed shrug emoticon, popular from about 2011.
biblical_def: IDK is the typed shrug. Sometimes it is simple honesty: I do not know the answer. Sometimes it is something else wearing honesty’s clothes: I do not want to decide, I do not want to think about it, I do not care enough to find out. The Christian observation separates the two. An honest "I don’t know" is a mark of wisdom and humility. Job, after all his speeches, confessed: "therefore have I uttered that I understood not; things too wonderful for me, which I knew not" (Job 42:3). Scripture honours the man who admits the edge of his knowledge, and it insists that some things belong to God alone: "The secret things belong unto the LORD our God: but those things which are revealed belong unto us and to our children for ever" (Deu 29:29). But the second half of that verse is a charge. What God has revealed, we are meant to know, and the shrug is no answer to the questions He has answered. Peter tells every believer to "be ready always to give an answer to every man that asketh you a reason of the hope that is in you" (1Pe 3:15). "If any of you lack wisdom, let him ask of God" (Jas 1:5). A father welcomes his child’s honest "I don’t know" and answers it with "let’s find out." He gently refuses the lazy "idk" on matters that need a decision, and he makes sure his children know what they believe and why.
webster_summary: Millennial text initialism (1990s–2000s) for I don’t know; honest humility when it marks the edge of knowledge (Deu 29:29), sloth when it shrugs off what God has revealed and asks us to answer (1Pe 3:15).
webster_full: IDK, interj. (Millennial text slang, 1990s–present; initialism of I don’t know) Ignorance, uncertainty, or reluctance to decide. Related: idek, idc, idrk, the shrug emoticon.

Webster (1828), root know: KNOW, verb transitive no. preterit tense knew; participle passive known. [Latin nosco, cognosco, Gr. although much varied in orthography. Nosco makes novi, which, with g or c prefixed, gnovi or cnovi, would coincide with know knew. So Latin cresco, crevi, coincides with grow, grew. The radical sense of knowing is generally to take, receive, or hold.] 1. To perceive with certainty; to understand clearly; to have a clear and certain perception of truth, fact, or any thing that actually exists. […]
Decode for parents: answer an honest idk with "let’s find out"; do not accept idk on what they believe.
scriptures: Job 42:3
Who is he that hideth counsel without knowledge? therefore have I uttered that I understood not; things too wonderful for me, which I knew not.
The secret things belong unto the LORD our God: but those things which are revealed belong unto us and to our children for ever, that we may do all the words of this law.
But sanctify the Lord God in your hearts: and be ready always to give an answer to every man that asketh you a reason of the hope that is in you with meekness and fear:
Jas 1:5
If any of you lack wisdom, let him ask of God, that giveth to all men liberally, and upbraideth not; and it shall be given him.

Yea, if thou criest after knowledge, and liftest up thy voice for understanding; If thou seekest her as silver, and searchest for her as for hid treasures; Then shalt thou understand the fear of the LORD, and find the knowledge of God.
corruption_summary: IDK can be humble honesty or a lazy shrug; Scripture honours the first and rebukes the second, because what God has revealed belongs to us and our children.
corruption_paragraphs: The drift is from honest ignorance to cultivated indifference. A generation with every fact in its pocket answers more questions with a shrug than any before it, because the shrug is not about information; it is about will. "I don’t know" becomes "don’t make me think," and in matters of faith it becomes a permanent posture: idk what I believe, idk if it matters. That is not humility. It is the sluggard’s answer to wisdom’s invitation.

Scripture’s remedy is the search. "If thou criest after knowledge, and liftest up thy voice for understanding; If thou seekest her as silver, and searchest for her as for hid treasures; Then shalt thou understand the fear of the LORD, and find the knowledge of God" (Pro 2:3-5). Teach the young that it is good to say "I don’t know," and better to follow it with prayer, study, and the courage to come to a conviction. Leave the secret things with God; take the revealed things home.
roots_summary: Old English cnawan (to know) → "I don’t know" → 1990s chat initialism idk → 2000s texting shrug (idek, idc).
roots_lines: Old English cnawan — to perceive, to recognize
1990s: chat initialism idk
2000s: texting; idek, idc, idrk
c. 2011: shrug emoticon as the visual idk
Biblical anchor: the secret things belong unto the LORD (Deu 29:29); be ready always to give an answer (1Pe 3:15)
usage: "Where do you want to eat?" "idk, wherever."
An honest idk is humble; a permanent one about the gospel is not (1Pe 3:15).
If any of you lack wisdom, let him ask of God (Jas 1:5).

etymology: Initialism for shaking my head, from mid-2000s online forums and early Twitter, mainstream on Twitter and Facebook by about 2010. It signals disappointment, disbelief, or disapproval at something foolish ("smh at these drivers"). Intensified as smdh (shaking my darn head; the vulgar version is common) and paired with the facepalm.
biblical_def: SMH reports a gesture: the slow head-shake of a person watching someone else do something foolish. It is the Millennial generation’s favourite one-word verdict on the news, the neighbours, and the comments section. The Christian observation: the head-shake appears in Scripture, and almost never kindly. At the cross, "they that passed by reviled him, wagging their heads" (Mat 27:39). The Psalmist, in the voice of the suffering Christ, says, "All they that see me laugh me to scorn: they shoot out the lip, they shake the head" (Psa 22:7). The shaken head is the posture of the spectator who judges and does nothing. There is a right grief at folly and sin; Lot "vexed his righteous soul from day to day with their unlawful deeds" (2Pe 2:8), and Jesus wept over Jerusalem. But righteous grief goes somewhere: to prayer, to warning, to rescue. Online, smh usually goes nowhere but up, a small badge of superiority. "Therefore thou art inexcusable, O man, whosoever thou art that judgest: for wherein thou judgest another, thou condemnest thyself" (Rom 2:1). A father teaches his children to grieve over sin, beginning with their own; to pray for the foolish rather than display their disdain; and to remember that the Lord who had every right to shake His head instead stretched out His hands.
webster_summary: Millennial online initialism (mid-2000s) for shaking my head; a spectator’s gesture of disdain that Scripture places on the lips of those who mocked the crucified Christ (Psa 22:7; Mat 27:39).
webster_full: SMH, interj. (Millennial online and text slang, mid-2000s–present; initialism of shaking my head) Expresses disappointment, disbelief, or disapproval. "Smh at people who don’t return carts." Intensive: smdh.

Webster (1828), root shake: SHAKE, verb transitive preterit tense shook ; participle passive shaken . 1. To cause to move with quick vibrations; to move rapidly one way and the other; to agitate; as, the wind shakes a tree; an earthquake shakes the hills or the earth. I shook my lap, and said, so God shake out every man from his house- Nehemiah 5:13 He shook the sacred honors of his head. Dryden . -As a fig casteth her untimely fruit, when it is shaken of a mighty wind. Revelation 6:1 . 2. To make to totter or tremble. […]
Decode for parents: the shaken head is a spectator’s verdict; teach children to pray and help instead of posting disdain.
scriptures: Psa 22:7
All they that see me laugh me to scorn: they shoot out the lip, they shake the head, saying,
And they that passed by reviled him, wagging their heads,
(For that righteous man dwelling among them, in seeing and hearing, vexed his righteous soul from day to day with their unlawful deeds;)
Rom 2:1
Therefore thou art inexcusable, O man, whosoever thou art that judgest: for wherein thou judgest another, thou condemnest thyself; for thou that judgest doest the same things.
And when he was come near, he beheld the city, and wept over it,
corruption_summary: SMH makes disdain a public badge; Scripture’s wagging heads belong to the mockers at Calvary, and righteous grief goes to prayer and rescue, not display.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is contempt as entertainment. Social media rewards the person who can most cleverly signal superiority to someone else’s folly, and smh is the cheapest form of that signal: it costs nothing, requires no help, and places the poster above the fray. The posture has a long biblical pedigree, and all of it is bad. It is the bystander at the cross, untouched, superior, wagging his head.

The recovery is the tears of Christ. "And when he was come near, he beheld the city, and wept over it" (Luk 19:41). The Lord saw the same folly the spectators saw, and He wept, warned, and went to die for it. That is the shape of righteous disapproval: grief that becomes intercession and action. Teach the young to notice folly without delighting in their own superiority, and when they feel the urge to shake their heads, to bow them instead.
roots_summary: Old English scacan (to shake) → "shaking my head" → mid-2000s forums and Black Twitter smh → c. 2010 mainstream.
roots_lines: Old English scacan — to move quickly to and fro
Mid-2000s: forum and Twitter initialism smh
c. 2010: mainstream on Twitter and Facebook; smdh, facepalm
Biblical image: the mockers "shake the head" (Psa 22:7; Mat 27:39)
Biblical recovery: he beheld the city, and wept over it (Luk 19:41)
usage: "Smh, he posted his test answers in the group chat."
The wagging heads stood at Calvary (Mat 27:39); bow yours instead.
Wherein thou judgest another, thou condemnest thyself (Rom 2:1).

etymology: Initialism for best friends forever, written in yearbooks and on notes passed in class since at least the 1980s, then universal in 2000s texting, MySpace "Top 8" friend rankings, and girls’ jewellery (the split-heart "BE FRI / ST ENDS" necklace). Paris Hilton’s reality show My New BFF (2008) marked the peak, and the major dictionaries admitted BFF in the early 2010s. Variants: bestie, BFFL (best friends for life).
biblical_def: A BFF is one’s best friend, sealed with the word forever. The initialism belongs to adolescence, especially to girls, and to the age of the ranked friend list, when a MySpace Top 8 could make or break a week. The Christian observation: the longing in the word is good and old. Scripture prizes deep friendship and gives us its great portrait. "The soul of Jonathan was knit with the soul of David, and Jonathan loved him as his own soul" (1Sa 18:1). "A friend loveth at all times, and a brother is born for adversity" (Pro 17:17). "There is a friend that sticketh closer than a brother" (Pro 18:24). The word’s weakness is the forever. Adolescent BFFs change with the school year, and the ranked list taught a generation that friendship is a status to be displayed and revised. Real friendship is proved over years and through trouble: "Faithful are the wounds of a friend" (Pro 27:6). And the only forever friendship on offer belongs to Christ: "Henceforth I call you not servants … but I have called you friends" (Joh 15:15). A father tells his daughter: a true friend is one who will tell you the truth and stay; pray for one, and be one. He tells his son: men need friends too, and the friend worth having will sharpen you, as iron sharpeneth iron.
webster_summary: Millennial initialism (1980s notes → 2000s texting) for best friends forever; redeemable as a longing for covenant friendship like David and Jonathan’s, whose only true forever is Christ’s friendship (Joh 15:15).
webster_full: BFF, n. (Millennial slang, 1980s–2010s; initialism of best friends forever) One’s closest friend. "She’s my BFF." Also bestie, BFFL; the split-heart BFF necklace.
Culture: MySpace "Top 8," My New BFF (2008); in the major dictionaries by the early 2010s.

Webster (1828), root friend: FRIEND, noun frend. 1. One who is attached to another by affection; one who entertains for another sentiments of esteem, respect and affection, which lead him to desire his company, and to seek to promote his happiness and prosperity; opposed to foe or enemy. A friend loveth at all times. Proverbs 17:17 . 2. One not hostile; opposed to an enemy in war. 3. One reconciled after enmity. Let us be friends again. 4. An attendant; a companion. 5. A favorer; one who is propitious; as a friend to commerce; a friend to poetry; […]
Decode for parents: teach your children to choose friends who sharpen them and to be the friend who stays.
scriptures: And it came to pass, when he had made an end of speaking unto Saul, that the soul of Jonathan was knit with the soul of David, and Jonathan loved him as his own soul.
A friend loveth at all times, and a brother is born for adversity.
A man that hath friends must shew himself friendly: and there is a friend that sticketh closer than a brother.
Pro 27:6
Faithful are the wounds of a friend; but the kisses of an enemy are deceitful.
Henceforth I call you not servants; for the servant knoweth not what his lord doeth: but I have called you friends; for all things that I have heard of my Father I have made known unto you.
corruption_summary: BFF turns friendship into a ranked, revisable status; Scripture’s friendship is a covenant proved in adversity, and its only true forever is the friendship of Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption came with the ranking. When friendship became a public list, it became a status game: who is in, who has been demoted, who is everyone’s BFF this month. Girls especially learned that friendship is a performance and that "forever" lasts until the next falling-out. The word promises a covenant and delivers a popularity chart, and the wound of being dropped from it is real.

The recovery is covenant friendship. Jonathan made a covenant with David and kept it at the cost of a throne; Ruth said to Naomi, "whither thou goest, I will go" (Rut 1:16) and meant it. Teach the young that friends are made by faithfulness, not by declaration; that a friend who wounds you with the truth loves you more than one who flatters; and that the Friend who laid down His life for His friends is the one whose forever is real.
roots_summary: Old English freond (one who loves) → best friends forever → 1980s notes and yearbooks → 2000s texting, MySpace Top 8 → dictionaries, early 2010s.
roots_lines: Old English freond, from freogan — to love, to favour
1980s: yearbook and note-passing initialism BFF
2000s: texting, MySpace Top 8, split-heart necklaces; My New BFF (2008)
Early 2010s: entered the major dictionaries; bestie as the spoken form
Biblical anchor: the soul of Jonathan was knit with the soul of David (1Sa 18:1); I have called you friends (Joh 15:15)
usage: "She’s been my BFF since second grade."
A friend loveth at all times (Pro 17:17); that is the forever in BFF.
Faithful are the wounds of a friend (Pro 27:6).

etymology: A blend of friend and enemy. Scattered uses go back to the mid-twentieth century: Walter Winchell’s syndicated column of May 1953 proposed calling the Russians our "frienemies." The Millennial word came from 1990s–2000s girl culture and television: Sex and the City used it in a 2000 episode, and the film Mean Girls (2004) dramatized the type without using the term. By the late 2000s it was standard slang for a rival who poses as a friend, and the business world adopted it for competitors who also cooperate.
biblical_def: A frenemy is a friend who is also an enemy: someone close enough to know your secrets and competitive enough to use them. The friendship is real enough to keep, and the rivalry is real enough to wound. Millennial culture treated the frenemy as an amusing fact of social life, especially among girls. The Christian observation: Scripture knows this person well and does not find him amusing. The sharpest grief in the Psalms is the betrayal of a frenemy: "For it was not an enemy that reproached me; then I could have borne it … But it was thou, a man mine equal, my guide, and mine acquaintance. We took sweet counsel together" (Psa 55:12-14). The supreme frenemy kissed his Lord in the garden: "Judas, betrayest thou the Son of man with a kiss?" (Luk 22:48). "The kisses of an enemy are deceitful" (Pro 27:6). James names the root: "For where envying and strife is, there is confusion and every evil work" (Jas 3:16), and calls the divided heart double-minded. The frenemy relationship is not a third category between friendship and enmity; it is enmity using friendship as cover. A father tells his children: do not keep a friend who is secretly glad when you fail, and above all do not be one. Love must be "without dissimulation" (Rom 12:9).
webster_summary: Millennial slang (1990s–2000s girl culture and TV; a friend + enemy blend) for a rival who poses as a friend; Scripture’s deepest grief is this betrayal, the deceitful kiss (Psa 55:12-14; Pro 27:6). Reject.
webster_full: FRENEMY, n. (Millennial slang, late 1990s–2010s; blend of friend + enemy) A person who acts as a friend while being a rival or secret antagonist. Also used of competitors that cooperate in business.

Webster (1828), root enemy: ENEMY, noun [Latin inimicus.] 1. A foe; an adversary. A private enemy is one who hates another and wishes him injury, or attempts to do him injury to gratify his own malice or ill will. A public enemy or foe, is one who belongs to a nation or party, at war with another. I way to you, love your enemies. Matthew 5:43 . Enemies in war; in peace friends. 2. One who hates or dislikes; as an enemy to truth or falsehood. 3. In theology, and by way of eminence, the enemy is the Devil; the archfiend. 4. […]
Decode for parents: ask your daughter whether any friend seems glad when she fails; envy dressed as friendship is the frenemy.
scriptures: For it was not an enemy that reproached me; then I could have borne it: neither was it he that hated me that did magnify himself against me; then I would have hid myself from him: But it was thou, a man mine equal, my guide, and mine acquaintance. We took sweet counsel together, and walked unto the house of God in company.
But Jesus said unto him, Judas, betrayest thou the Son of man with a kiss?
Pro 27:6
Faithful are the wounds of a friend; but the kisses of an enemy are deceitful.
Jas 3:16
For where envying and strife is, there is confusion and every evil work.
Rom 12:9
Let love be without dissimulation. Abhor that which is evil; cleave to that which is good.
corruption_summary: Frenemy normalizes enmity disguised as friendship; Scripture names it betrayal, the deceitful kiss, and requires love without dissimulation.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is that the word makes treachery ordinary. By giving the double-minded friendship a cute name, the culture stopped being shocked by it; girls in particular were taught that rivalry, gossip, and quiet sabotage are simply how friendship works. Scripture will not file it under social life. It is envy, and envy is "the rottenness of the bones" (Pro 14:30). The frenemy’s smile is a Judas kiss in miniature.

The recovery is single-hearted love. "Let love be without dissimulation. Abhor that which is evil; cleave to that which is good" (Rom 12:9). A Christian may compete hard and still rejoice when a rival does well; he may not pretend friendship while hoping for a fall. Teach the young to examine their own hearts for envy before they diagnose anyone else, to choose friends who rejoice with them that rejoice, and to end a frenemy relationship honestly rather than continuing a show.
roots_summary: Friend + enemy → scattered mid-20th-c. coinages → 1990s–2000s girl culture and TV (Sex and the City, 2000) → late-2000s standard slang.
roots_lines: Old English freond (friend) + Latin inimicus (not a friend) → enemy
1953: Walter Winchell’s column, "frienemies," of the Soviet Union
2000: Sex and the City popularizes it; 2004: Mean Girls dramatizes the type
Late 2000s: general slang; business sense for cooperating competitors
Biblical anchor: it was not an enemy that reproached me (Psa 55:12); the kisses of an enemy are deceitful (Pro 27:6)
usage: "She’s nice to my face, but she’s totally a frenemy."
It was not an enemy that reproached me; it was thou, mine acquaintance (Psa 55:12-13).
Let love be without dissimulation (Rom 12:9).

etymology: A blend of brother (via bro) and romance, coined in the 1990s by Dave Carnie, editor of the skateboarding magazine Big Brother, for the close friendships between skaters who spent all their time together. It went mainstream in the late 2000s through film and television: the "bromantic comedies" I Love You, Man (2009) and the Judd Apatow cycle, and MTV’s Bromance (2008). It was added to major dictionaries by 2010.
biblical_def: A bromance is a close, affectionate friendship between two men, described half-jokingly in the vocabulary of romance. The word arrived when popular culture had begun to find male friendship awkward: men could be buddies, but deep affection between them needed a joke attached. The Christian observation: the thing named is good, and the name is confused. Scripture honours deep friendship between men without embarrassment. "The soul of Jonathan was knit with the soul of David" (1Sa 18:1), and at Jonathan’s death David lamented, "very pleasant hast thou been unto me: thy love to me was wonderful" (2Sa 1:26). The Lord Jesus had a disciple "whom he loved," who leaned on His breast at supper. "Iron sharpeneth iron; so a man sharpeneth the countenance of his friend" (Pro 27:17). But that love is philia, brotherly love, and the word romance blurs the line Scripture keeps clear between friendship and the love of a man for his wife. A culture that can only name deep male friendship as a kind of romance will eventually suspect all of it, and many young men, fearing the suspicion, settle for no close friends at all. A father tells his son: you need brothers, men you pray with, confess to, and fight beside. Call it what it is, friendship, and do not let anyone make you ashamed of it.
webster_summary: Millennial slang (1990s skate culture; late-2000s film) for a close friendship between men, framed jokingly as romance; the friendship is biblical (1Sa 18:1; Pro 27:17), the romance framing confuses philia with marital love.
webster_full: BROMANCE, n. (Millennial slang, 1990s–2010s; blend of bro + romance) A close, affectionate, non-sexual friendship between two men. Also bromantic, "bromantic comedy."

Webster (1828), root romance: ROMANCE, noun romans’, ro’mans. 1. A fabulous relation or story of adventures and incidents, designed for the entertainment of readers; a tale of extraordinary adventures, fictitious and often extravagant, usually a tale of love or war, subjects interesting the sensibilities of the heart, or the passions of wonder and curiosity. romance differs from the novel, as it treats of great actions and extraordinary adventures; […]
Decode for parents: your son needs real brothers; teach him to name it friendship and pursue it unashamed.
scriptures: And it came to pass, when he had made an end of speaking unto Saul, that the soul of Jonathan was knit with the soul of David, and Jonathan loved him as his own soul.
I am distressed for thee, my brother Jonathan: very pleasant hast thou been unto me: thy love to me was wonderful, passing the love of women.
Iron sharpeneth iron; so a man sharpeneth the countenance of his friend.
Now there was leaning on Jesus' bosom one of his disciples, whom Jesus loved.

Two are better than one; because they have a good reward for their labour. For if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow: but woe to him that is alone when he falleth; for he hath not another to help him up.
corruption_summary: Bromance names good male friendship in the vocabulary of romance; the joke breeds suspicion, and the suspicion leaves young men friendless.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is in the frame. By describing male friendship as quasi-romance, the culture treated deep affection between men as either comic or suspect, and in the years since, the suspicion has hardened. Revisionists now read David and Jonathan through the same lens, which is exactly backward: Scripture presents their love as the model of covenant friendship, and its world kept friendship and marriage distinct. Meanwhile young men, unwilling to be mocked, retreat into isolation, games, and screens.

The recovery is an unembarrassed recovery of brotherhood. "Two are better than one … For if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow" (Ecc 4:9-10). Men in the Church should have friends who know their sins, share their burdens, and sharpen their faith. Teach the young that a man with brothers is stronger, that affection between friends is no shame, and that the right word for it is the old one: friendship, brotherly love, philadelphia.
roots_summary: Brother → bro + Old French romanz (romance) → 1990s skate-magazine coinage → 2008–2009 film and TV → dictionaries by 2010.
roots_lines: Old English brothor → 20th-c. clipped bro
Old French romanz — a tale in the vernacular, later a love story
1990s: Dave Carnie, Big Brother magazine, coins bromance
2008–2009: MTV’s Bromance; I Love You, Man; the "bromantic comedy"
Biblical anchor: the soul of Jonathan was knit with the soul of David (1Sa 18:1); iron sharpeneth iron (Pro 27:17)
usage: "Those two have had a bromance since boot camp."
Call it friendship: iron sharpeneth iron (Pro 27:17).
Two are better than one; if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow (Ecc 4:9-10).

etymology: A room or space in a house set apart for a man’s leisure: a basement, garage, or den with a big television, sports memorabilia, a bar or gaming setup. The phrase appears in 1990s newspaper real-estate and lifestyle writing; John Gray’s Men Are from Mars, Women Are from Venus (1992) had popularized the idea that men "retreat to their caves" to process stress. Home-improvement television (Man Caves, DIY Network, 2007–2011) and Millennial homebuying culture made it a standard real-estate feature and decorating category.
biblical_def: A man cave is a husband’s or father’s private retreat within the home, a room furnished for his hobbies and his rest, where the rest of the family visits by invitation. The Christian observation: there is nothing wrong with a workshop, a study, or a place to watch a game with friends. Rest is God’s gift, and the Lord Jesus Himself withdrew to quiet places to pray. But the phrase carries a theory with it, that a man naturally retreats into a cave and that his family should leave him there. Scripture has a famous man in a cave. Elijah, exhausted and afraid, fled to Horeb, "And he came thither unto a cave, and lodged there; and, behold, the word of the LORD came to him, and he said unto him, What doest thou here, Elijah?" (1Ki 19:9). God fed him and let him rest, and then sent him back out with work to do. The cave was a place to recover, not a place to live. A husband is told to "dwell with them according to knowledge" (1Pe 3:7), and a father is told to teach his children "when thou sittest in thine house" (Deu 6:7). Fathers are not excused from the life of the house. A father with a man cave should ask: does my family know where to find me, and do they want to come in? Make the room a place your sons are welcome, where you teach them to fix things, and the cave becomes a workshop for manhood.
webster_summary: Millennial-era slang (1990s, popularized 2000s) for a man’s private leisure room in the home; rest is good, but Elijah’s cave was a place to recover and be sent out (1Ki 19:9), not a hiding place from family.
webster_full: MAN CAVE, n. (slang, 1990s; Millennial homebuying and decorating term, 2000s–2010s) A room set apart for a man’s leisure and hobbies: a den, basement, or garage with television, games, and memorabilia. Counterpart coinage: she shed.

Webster (1828), root cave: CAVE, noun A hollow place in the earth; a subterraneous cavern; a den. This may be natural or artificial. The primitive inhabitants of the earth, in many countries, lived in caves; and the present inhabitants of some parts of the earth, especially in the high northern latitudes, occupy caves, particularly in winter. Lot dwelt in a cave he and his daughters. Genesis 19:30 . CAVE s were also used for the burial of the dead. Abraham buried Sarah in the cave of the field of Machpelab. Genesis 23:9 . […]
Decode for parents: a man cave can be a workshop for sons or a bunker from family; the difference is whether the door is open.
scriptures: And he came thither unto a cave, and lodged there; and, behold, the word of the LORD came to him, and he said unto him, What doest thou here, Elijah?

Likewise, ye husbands, dwell with them according to knowledge, giving honour unto the wife, as unto the weaker vessel, and as being heirs together of the grace of life; that your prayers be not hindered.
Deu 6:7
And thou shalt teach them diligently unto thy children, and shalt talk of them when thou sittest in thine house, and when thou walkest by the way, and when thou liest down, and when thou risest up.
Mar 1:35
And in the morning, rising up a great while before day, he went out, and departed into a solitary place, and there prayed.
Lo, children are an heritage of the LORD: and the fruit of the womb is his reward.
corruption_summary: Man cave can bless a man’s rest, or it can enshrine retreat from his household; Scripture lets Elijah rest in the cave and then asks, What doest thou here?
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the theory behind the room: that withdrawal is a man’s natural mode and that his family’s demands are something to be escaped. A generation of fathers was told, in effect, that they could build a bunker within their own house. The cultural results are familiar: fathers present in body and absent in attention, sons raised by screens a wall away from a father watching his own. Scripture never calls a man to that kind of absence. It calls him to dwell with his wife with understanding and to raise his children in the nurture and admonition of the Lord.

The redemption is rest that returns to work. "And in the morning, rising up a great while before day, he went out, and departed into a solitary place, and there prayed" (Mar 1:35). The Lord withdrew to be with His Father and came back to serve. A Christian man may have a study, a workshop, or a den; let it be a place where he prays, where he rests to serve again, and where his children are welcome. "Lo, children are an heritage of the LORD" (Psa 127:3); a heritage is not something you hide from.
roots_summary: Latin cavus (hollow) → cave → 1990s "man cave" (with Gray’s retreat-to-the-cave theory) → 2007–2011 TV Man Caves → real-estate standard.
roots_lines: Latin cavus — hollow; cave — a hollow place in the earth
1992: John Gray’s "men retreat to their caves"
1990s–2000s: man cave in real-estate and lifestyle writing
2007–2011: DIY Network’s Man Caves; counterpart she shed
Biblical anchor: What doest thou here, Elijah? (1Ki 19:9)
usage: "The basement’s going to be my man cave."
Elijah rested in the cave, then God sent him out (1Ki 19:9).
A father’s den should have an open door for his sons (Deu 6:7).

etymology: Originally military aviation: the pilot who flies off the leader’s wing and protects him in combat (US usage from the 1940s–50s, popularized by Korean War and Vietnam-era air combat). Civilian slang borrowed it for the friend who accompanies a man at a bar or party and helps him meet women, typically by occupying the woman’s friends. The film Top Gun (1986) put the aviation sense in every boy’s head; Millennial dating culture of the 2000s (and later dating apps with "wingman" features) made the social sense dominant.
biblical_def: A wingman, in social slang, is the friend who helps you approach a woman: he talks you up, distracts her friends, and gives you courage. In the military, he is the pilot who guards your blind spot. The Christian observation: the military sense is closer to the biblical ideal of friendship, and the social sense depends entirely on what the wingman is helping with. Scripture has a remarkable "wingman" story: Abraham’s servant, sent to find a wife for Isaac, who prayed, "O LORD God of my master Abraham, I pray thee, send me good speed this day" (Gen 24:12), and was led to Rebekah. Boaz’s honourable pursuit of Ruth happened in public, at the gate, before witnesses. Those are models of helping a man find a wife. The bar-scene wingman is usually helping with something else: a night’s conquest, a phone number for a hookup. Then he is not a friend but an accomplice, and Scripture warns, "My son, if sinners entice thee, consent thou not" (Pro 1:10). The best wingman protects his friend’s blind spot, including his blind spot for sin. "Two are better than one … For if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow" (Ecc 4:9-10). A father tells his son: get friends who will help you find a godly wife and who will pull you out of the room when you are about to do something stupid. And be that kind of wingman.
webster_summary: Military aviation term turned Millennial dating slang for the friend who helps a man meet women; honourable when he helps a friend seek a wife (Gen 24:12), an accomplice when he helps a hookup (Pro 1:10).
webster_full: WINGMAN, n. (military aviation, 1940s–; Millennial dating slang, 2000s–2010s) (1) The pilot who flies beside and protects the leader. (2) A friend who helps a man approach and impress a woman, often by engaging her companions. Feminine: wingwoman.

Webster (1828), root wing: WING, noun 1. The limb of a fowl by which it flies. In a few species of fowls, the wings do not enable them to fly; as is the case with the dodo, ostrich, great auk, and penguin; but in the two former, the wings assist the fowls in running. 2. The limb of an insect by which it flies. 3. In botany, the side petal of a papilionaceous corol; also, an appendage of seeds, by means of which they are wafted in the air and scattered; […]
Decode for parents: ask your son what his friends help him do; a true wingman guards your blind spots, including sin.
scriptures: And he said, O LORD God of my master Abraham, I pray thee, send me good speed this day, and shew kindness unto my master Abraham.
Pro 1:10
My son, if sinners entice thee, consent thou not.

Two are better than one; because they have a good reward for their labour. For if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow: but woe to him that is alone when he falleth; for he hath not another to help him up.
He that walketh with wise men shall be wise: but a companion of fools shall be destroyed.
Rut 4:10

Moreover Ruth the Moabitess, the wife of Mahlon, have I purchased to be my wife, to raise up the name of the dead upon his inheritance, that the name of the dead be not cut off from among his brethren, and from the gate of his place: ye are witnesses this day.
corruption_summary: The social wingman too often helps a friend pursue a conquest; the biblical friend guards your blind spots and helps you seek a wife honourably.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is friendship turned into complicity. The bar-scene wingman exists to help a man get what he wants for the night, and his loyalty is measured by how well he serves that want. That inverts what a friend is for. "He that walketh with wise men shall be wise: but a companion of fools shall be destroyed" (Pro 13:20). The wingman who helps you sin is walking you toward destruction with a smile and a high-five.

The recovery returns to the aviation meaning: protection in a fight. The Christian young man needs friends who cover his blind spots, who pray with him about marriage, who encourage honourable pursuit, and who will stand between him and the temptation he is not seeing. Boaz’s pursuit of Ruth was public and witnessed: "Ruth the Moabitess … have I purchased to be my wife … ye are witnesses this day" (Rut 4:10). Teach the young to want friends who would be glad to stand as those witnesses.
roots_summary: Old Norse vængr (wing) → aviation wingman (1940s–50s) → Top Gun (1986) → 2000s dating slang.
roots_lines: Old Norse vængr → Middle English wenge — wing
1940s–50s: US military aviation, the leader’s protector
1986: Top Gun popularizes the term
2000s: dating slang for the helping friend; wingwoman
Biblical anchor: the servant who prayed for good speed (Gen 24:12); if sinners entice thee, consent thou not (Pro 1:10)
usage: "Be my wingman tonight; her friend is cool."
A true wingman guards your blind spot, sin included (Ecc 4:10).
A companion of fools shall be destroyed (Pro 13:20).

etymology: Popularized by the American sitcom Friends in a 1994 episode ("The One with the Blackout"), in which Joey tells Ross he has waited too long to make a move on Rachel and is now "mayor of the zone." By the 2000s friend zone (noun) and to friend-zone (verb) were standard Millennial slang for a person, usually a man, who wants romance but is kept as "just a friend." In the 2010s the phrase drew criticism for implying that a woman’s friendship is a consolation prize or a debt.
biblical_def: To be friend-zoned is to want a romantic relationship and be told, gently or by drift, that one is only a friend. The phrase is usually spoken with grievance: the "nice guy" who did everything right and got nothing. The Christian observation has two edges. On one side, unrequited love is a real sorrow and deserves compassion; the young man who has hoped and been disappointed is not a joke. On the other side, the phrase smuggles in a bad theory: that friendship is a waiting room for romance, that kindness is an investment owed a return, and that a woman who says no has done something to him. Scripture rejects all three. Love "seeketh not her own" (1Co 13:5). Friendship is a good in itself, not a lesser prize: "A friend loveth at all times" (Pro 17:17). And a man who is kind in order to collect is practising the transaction Jesus condemned: "if ye do good to them which do good to you, what thank have ye?" (Luk 6:33). The healthier path is also the more honest one: say what you hope for, and accept the answer. "Let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay" (Mat 5:37). A father tells his son: if you want to court a girl, say so, respectfully; if she says no, remain a gentleman and a friend if she wants one, and trust God with your future. He tells his daughter: you never owe a boy romance because he was nice to you.
webster_summary: Millennial slang (Friends, 1994) for being kept as "just a friend" by someone one desires; real sorrow, wrapped in a bad theory that treats friendship as a consolation prize and kindness as a debt (1Co 13:5). Reject the framing.
webster_full: FRIEND ZONE, n.; FRIEND-ZONE, v.t. (Millennial slang, 1994–present) The state of being regarded only as a friend by someone one wishes to date; to keep such a person as a friend. "He got friend-zoned."
Criticized in the 2010s for implying a woman owes romance in return for friendship.

Webster (1828), root zone: ZONE, noun [Latin , Gr.] 1. A girdle. An embroiderd zone surrounds her waist. 2. In geography, a division of the earth, with respect to the temperature of different latitudes. The zones are five; the torrid zone extending from tropic to tropic 46 degrees, 56 degrees, or 23 degrees 28’ on each side of the equator; two temperate or variable zones, situated between the tropics and polar circles; and two frigid zones, situated between the polar circles and the poles. 3. Circuit; circumference. […]
Decode for parents: teach sons to pursue honestly and accept no gracefully; teach daughters they owe no one romance.
scriptures: Doth not behave itself unseemly, seeketh not her own, is not easily provoked, thinketh no evil;
A friend loveth at all times, and a brother is born for adversity.
Luk 6:33
And if ye do good to them which do good to you, what thank have ye? for sinners also do even the same.
Mat 5:37
But let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay: for whatsoever is more than these cometh of evil.
Pro 16:9
A man's heart deviseth his way: but the LORD directeth his steps.
corruption_summary: Friend zone treats friendship as a waiting room and kindness as a debt; Scripture’s love seeketh not her own, and honest pursuit accepts an honest no.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is entitlement dressed as heartbreak. The friend-zone complaint assumes that attention and favours obligate a return, and that a woman who declines has cheated the man who invested in her. That is not love but commerce, and the resentment it breeds has curdled in the darker corners of the internet into open contempt for women. Even in milder forms, it trains young men to be indirect, to hope that niceness will slowly purchase what they never honestly asked for.

The recovery is courage and contentment. Biblical pursuit is open; Boaz did not wait in a "zone" but went to the gate. And biblical friendship is not a second prize: Christ calls His disciples friends, and there is no higher honour. Teach young men to declare their intentions honestly, to hear no with grace, and to trust that "A man’s heart deviseth his way: but the LORD directeth his steps" (Pro 16:9). A man who can be a true friend after a refusal is the kind of man worth marrying.
roots_summary: Greek zōnē (girdle, belt) → zone → 1994 Friends ("mayor of the zone") → 2000s noun and verb → 2010s critique.
roots_lines: Greek zōnē — a girdle; Latin zona — a belt, a region
1994: Friends, "The One with the Blackout"
2000s: friend zone (n.), friend-zone (v.)
2010s: critique of its entitlement; "nice guy" discourse
Biblical anchor: charity seeketh not her own (1Co 13:5); a friend loveth at all times (Pro 17:17)
usage: "I helped her move twice and she still friend-zoned me."
Love seeketh not her own (1Co 13:5); kindness is not a down payment.
Say what you hope for, and let your nay be nay (Mat 5:37).

etymology: From cuffed (handcuffed, i.e. tied down in a relationship), hip-hop and African-American slang of the 2000s. Cuffing season appeared on Twitter and Urban Dictionary around 2011 for the colder months, roughly October through February, when singles supposedly seek a short-term partner for the holidays and winter nights, then "uncuff" in spring. Fabolous’s song "Cuffing Season" (2013) and seasonal news features spread it; dating apps now report a measurable autumn rise in activity.
biblical_def: Cuffing season is the cold-weather pairing-up: from late autumn to Valentine’s Day, singles look for a partner to bring home for Thanksgiving, to take to holiday parties, and to stay in with on winter nights, with an understood expiration date in spring. The Christian observation: the phrase is candid about its premise, and the premise is the problem. It describes relationships chosen for convenience and comfort, sized to a season, with the exit planned from the start. Scripture’s pattern is covenant, not season. "Therefore shall a man leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife: and they shall be one flesh" (Gen 2:24). The love Scripture describes "beareth all things, believeth all things, hopeth all things, endureth all things" (1Co 13:7), not until the thaw. Behind cuffing season usually lies a sexual relationship without covenant, which Scripture calls fornication: "Flee fornication" (1Co 6:18). And the loneliness that drives it is real; but Scripture answers loneliness with the household of God, where "God setteth the solitary in families" (Psa 68:6), not with a temporary partner. A father tells his son: never ask a woman for a winter; ask her for a lifetime or nothing. He tells his daughter: a man who wants you for a season does not want you; wait for the one who wants your whole life and will say so in front of witnesses.
webster_summary: Millennial slang (c. 2011, from hip-hop cuffed) for the autumn–winter pairing-up of singles in relationships meant to expire in spring; convenience love with a planned exit, against covenant (Gen 2:24). Reject.
webster_full: CUFFING SEASON, n. (Millennial slang, c. 2011–present; from cuffed, tied down in a relationship) The colder months, roughly October to February, when singles seek a temporary partner. Also to cuff, cuffed, uncuffing.
Webster (1828), root cuff: CUFF, noun [This word probably signifies a fold or doubling.] The fold at the end of a sleeve; the part of a sleeve turned back from the hand.
Decode for parents: the phrase names a relationship with a planned exit; teach your children to want a covenant.
scriptures: Gen 2:24
Therefore shall a man leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife: and they shall be one flesh.
Beareth all things, believeth all things, hopeth all things, endureth all things.
Flee fornication. Every sin that a man doeth is without the body; but he that committeth fornication sinneth against his own body.
Psa 68:6
God setteth the solitary in families: he bringeth out those which are bound with chains: but the rebellious dwell in a dry land.
Mal 2:14
Yet ye say, Wherefore? Because the LORD hath been witness between thee and the wife of thy youth, against whom thou hast dealt treacherously: yet is she thy companion, and the wife of thy covenant.
corruption_summary: Cuffing season names relationships sized to a season with the exit planned in advance; Scripture’s love is covenant, cleaving, and enduring all things.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is planned impermanence. Earlier generations sinned against marriage too, but cuffing season builds the breakup into the beginning and calls it normal. It trains the young to treat another person as a seasonal comfort, like a heavy coat, and to practise intimacy without commitment until commitment itself looks strange. That is preparation not for marriage but for divorce. God calls the marriage bond a covenant and Himself its witness: "the LORD hath been witness between thee and the wife of thy youth … yet is she thy companion, and the wife of thy covenant" (Mal 2:14).

The recovery is to take loneliness to the right place. The cold months are lonely, and the Church should be the warmest house in town: tables full of singles, widows, and students for Thanksgiving and Christmas, so that no one needs to rent a partner for the holidays. And the young should be taught that the man or woman worth having will offer covenant, not a lease. Courtship toward marriage is the opposite of cuffing: it begins with the end in view and means it.
roots_summary: Old English / Middle English cuffe (sleeve end) → handcuffs → 2000s hip-hop cuffed → c. 2011 cuffing season → 2013 Fabolous song.
roots_lines: Middle English cuffe — a glove, then the end of a sleeve
Handcuffs → slang cuffed — tied down, in a committed relationship
c. 2011: cuffing season on Twitter and Urban Dictionary
2013: Fabolous, "Cuffing Season"; annual news and dating-app features
Biblical anchor: cleave unto his wife (Gen 2:24); charity endureth all things (1Co 13:7)
usage: "It’s October. Cuffing season’s here."
Do not ask for a winter; ask for a lifetime (Gen 2:24).
God setteth the solitary in families (Psa 68:6): the Church’s answer to the lonely months.

etymology: From the dating app Tinder (launched 2012; the swipe became its signature gesture by 2013), where a user swipes a profile photo left to reject and right to express interest; mutual right-swipes create a "match." By 2014 swipe left was general slang for rejecting anything quickly and on appearance ("swipe left on that idea"), and swipe right for approval. Bumble, Hinge, and others adopted the gesture, which made appearance-first judgment the default interface of Millennial dating.
biblical_def: To swipe left is to reject, originally a person on a dating app, in about a second, on the basis of a photo and a line of text. The gesture has become a figure of speech for any snap dismissal. The Christian observation: the interface trains a habit of soul. It teaches the user to judge people by their outward appearance, instantly, at scale, and without consequence, hundreds of image-bearers dismissed in an evening. Scripture has a sentence written against exactly this: "Look not on his countenance, or on the height of his stature … for the LORD seeth not as man seeth; for man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart" (1Sa 16:7). James rebukes the same habit in church: "are ye not then partial in yourselves, and are become judges of evil thoughts?" (Jas 2:4). The Lord Jesus told us to "Judge not according to the appearance, but judge righteous judgment" (Joh 7:24). There is a place for discernment, and not every match should be pursued; but character, faith, and faithfulness cannot be seen in a thumbnail. A father tells his son: the girl you would swipe past in a second may be the one who would pray for you for fifty years; get to know women in real life, in the church, among families, where the heart can be seen. He tells his daughter: no one who judged you by a photo knows you.
webster_summary: Millennial slang (Tinder, 2012) for rejecting a person, or anything, at a glance; an interface that trains judgment by appearance, against the Lord who looketh on the heart (1Sa 16:7).
webster_full: SWIPE LEFT, v. (Millennial dating-app slang, 2012–present) To reject a profile on a dating app by swiping its photo left; by extension, to dismiss anything quickly. Opposite: swipe right.
Webster (1828), root swipe: SWIPE, noun A swape or sweep, which see.
Decode for parents: an evening of swiping is an evening of judging image-bearers by a photo; teach children to meet people where the heart can be seen.
scriptures: But the LORD said unto Samuel, Look not on his countenance, or on the height of his stature; because I have refused him: for the LORD seeth not as man seeth; for man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart.
Jas 2:4
Are ye not then partial in yourselves, and are become judges of evil thoughts?
Joh 7:24
Judge not according to the appearance, but judge righteous judgment.
Favour is deceitful, and beauty is vain: but a woman that feareth the LORD, she shall be praised.
Gen 1:27
So God created man in his own image, in the image of God created he him; male and female created he them.
corruption_summary: Swipe left trains the soul to judge image-bearers instantly by appearance; Scripture says the LORD looketh on the heart and commands righteous judgment.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is in the habit, not the single gesture. Hundreds of rapid judgments on faces teach the heart that people are products and that the outward appearance is the decisive fact. The user grows pickier and lonelier at once, and the rejected learn that they were dismissed in a second for their looks. Every face on that screen is someone made in God’s image: "So God created man in his own image" (Gen 1:27). An interface that makes dismissing them effortless is forming its users, whether they notice or not.

The recovery is to put knowing back before judging. In Scripture marriages begin among families and communities, where reputation, character, and faith are known. Teach the young that a spouse is chosen for the fear of the Lord, for "Favour is deceitful, and beauty is vain: but a woman that feareth the LORD, she shall be praised" (Pro 31:30), and that such things are learned over time and in person. If they use apps at all, let them use them as introductions, not verdicts.
roots_summary: Swipe (a sweeping blow) → touchscreen swipe gesture → Tinder (2012) left = reject → 2014 general slang for snap dismissal.
roots_lines: Swipe, variant of sweep — a sweeping stroke or blow
2007–2010: touchscreen swipe gestures
2012–2013: Tinder launches; its left (reject) / right (interest) swipe becomes the signature
2014–: general slang; Bumble, Hinge adopt the gesture
Biblical anchor: man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart (1Sa 16:7)
usage: "Gym selfie with a fish? Swipe left."
The LORD seeth not as man seeth (1Sa 16:7).
Judge not according to the appearance, but judge righteous judgment (Joh 7:24).

etymology: Initialism for define the relationship, the conversation in which two people dating decide what they are to each other: exclusive or not, boyfriend and girlfriend or "just talking." The phrase is widely associated with 1990s evangelical college campuses, where the "DTR talk" was a rite of passage; it spread through 2000s dating culture, and became essential in the 2010s app era of situationships, "talking stages," and ambiguous hookups, when the default was to leave everything undefined.
biblical_def: A DTR is the conversation where a couple stops guessing and says out loud what they are to each other. The Millennial dating world needed a name for it because so much of that world was designed to avoid it: hanging out, talking, seeing where it goes, never saying. The Christian observation: the instinct behind the DTR is righteous and sorely needed. Scripture prizes clarity in relationships between men and women. The Lord Jesus said, "let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay" (Mat 5:37). Ruth asked Boaz plainly at the threshing floor, "spread therefore thy skirt over thine handmaid; for thou art a near kinsman" (Rut 3:9), and Boaz answered just as plainly and acted the next morning. Rebekah was asked, "Wilt thou go with this man? And she said, I will go" (Gen 24:58). Biblical courtship is a long DTR: a man declares his intention toward marriage, families are involved, and both know where they stand. What the Millennial DTR often lacks is a destination; it defines the relationship as "exclusive" without asking "toward what?" A father tells his son: if you are spending time alone with a girl, you owe her and her father a definition, and the honest one is "I am considering marriage." He tells his daughter: if a boy will not define it, he has defined it already.
webster_summary: Millennial slang (1990s, associated with Christian colleges) for define the relationship; redeemable as the honest clarity Scripture prizes (Mat 5:37; Rut 3:9), best when the definition points toward marriage.
webster_full: DTR, n. (Millennial dating slang, 1990s–present; initialism of define the relationship) The conversation in which a dating couple clarifies their status and intentions. "We had the DTR last night." Contrast situationship, "talking stage."

Webster (1828), root define: DEFINE, verb transitive [Latin To end, to limit, from finis, end.] 1. To determine or describe the end or limit; as, to define the extent of a kingdom or country. 2. To determine with precision; to ascertain; as, to define the limits of a kingdom. 3. To mark the limit; to circumscribe; to bound. 4. To determine or ascertain the extent of the meaning of a word; to ascertain the signification of a term; to explain what a word is understood to express; as, to define the words, virtue, courage, belief, or charity. 5. […]
Decode for parents: if your child cannot say what a relationship is, it needs a DTR, and the best definition names marriage as the aim.
scriptures: Mat 5:37
But let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay: for whatsoever is more than these cometh of evil.
Rut 3:9
And he said, Who art thou? And she answered, I am Ruth thine handmaid: spread therefore thy skirt over thine handmaid; for thou art a near kinsman.
And they called Rebekah, and said unto her, Wilt thou go with this man? And she said, I will go.
Hope deferred maketh the heart sick: but when the desire cometh, it is a tree of life.
That no man go beyond and defraud his brother in any matter: because that the Lord is the avenger of all such, as we also have forewarned you and testified.
corruption_summary: DTR rightly demands clarity in a dating culture built on ambiguity; its weakness is a definition with no destination, and Scripture’s definition points to covenant.
corruption_paragraphs: The need for the DTR exposes the disease of modern dating: deliberate ambiguity. Relationships drift for months without anyone saying what they are, which keeps options open for the one with less at stake and leaves the other in limbo. "Hope deferred maketh the heart sick" (Pro 13:12). The ambiguity is not neutral. Paul warns "That no man go beyond and defraud his brother in any matter" (1Th 4:6), in a passage about sexual purity; to take the affection of someone while withholding a commitment is a kind of fraud.

The redemption is to make the definition early and honest, and to give it a direction. Christian courtship is not a series of DTRs, each one a little more exclusive, but a single declared purpose: I am pursuing you toward marriage, and I will do it openly. Teach the young that clarity is kindness, that the honest no is better than months of maybe, and that the best relationship definitions are spoken at last in vows.
roots_summary: Latin definire (to set bounds) → define → 1990s Christian-college DTR → 2000s–2010s mainstream dating slang.
roots_lines: Latin definire — to limit, to set bounds, to explain
1990s: the "DTR talk," widely associated with evangelical college campuses
2000s–2010s: general dating slang; the "DTR talk"
Contrast: situationship, "talking stage" — relationships left undefined
Biblical anchor: let your communication be, Yea, yea (Mat 5:37); spread thy skirt over thine handmaid (Rut 3:9)
usage: "We’ve been hanging out for three months. Time for the DTR."
Ruth’s DTR at the threshing floor was plain, and Boaz answered by morning (Rut 3:9).
Hope deferred maketh the heart sick (Pro 13:12): define it.
